note: Dense clonal stand of tall goldenrod in a field edge, with early yellow panicles just opening at upper left and the characteristic single unbranched stems densely clothed in narrow, alternate, sharply toothed lance-shaped leaves. Rubus canes with palmate/trifoliate toothed leaves fill the lower left foreground.

Screened out: The subject of this photograph is an animal (a small land snail) resting on a leaf; the vegetation is only background context and no diagnostic plant features (flowers, fruit, stem, leaf arrangement) are shown.

Wide habitat shot of a late-summer old-field/meadow edge dominated by plume-flowered yellow goldenrod (Solidago), with flat-topped white composites (likely flat-topped white aster or boneset) mixed in and a young hardwood edge behind. Identified to genus only — no close view of leaves or stems, so species-level goldenrod ID is not supportable from this frame; nothing here suggests a watchlist invasive, though a closer look at any tall clumped stems with hollow, jointed canes would be needed to rule out Japanese knotweed in a field like this.

Habitat/structure shot: a large hardwood snag with a heart-rot cavity and a broken limb, in an open mixed-hardwood stand. No leaves are attached to the dead trunk and the bark is too weathered to key — no foliage, twig, or bud detail to separate maple, ash, or oak, so I can only record it as an unidentified hardwood snag. Background canopy foliage is small and glossy (possibly beech/birch) but not resolvable at this distance.

Dense mat of pleurocarpous and acrocarpous mosses with pale blue-green lichen (likely a Cladonia squamule crust or Hypogymnia-type foliose lichen) covering the base and buttress of a tree trunk. No capsules, leaf detail, or apothecia are visible at this resolution, so the mosses can only be logged as a mixed bryophyte community rather than identified to genus. [Catalogue entry "Mixed Moss and Lichen Mat (tree base)" removed: "mixed" in the name — a description of the photo, not a taxon. This photo remains unidentified.]

Close-up of a mossy tree trunk/log with pale grey-green squamulose basal scales and several stalked, flaring trumpet- or goblet-shaped podetia — classic Cladonia (pixie cup / trumpet lichen). Species-level ID would need cup margin detail (proliferating vs. entire) and chemical spot tests, so left at genus.

Pale grey-green pixie-cup lichens (Cladonia sp., trumpet/goblet-shaped podetia rising from a squamulose basal thallus) growing among moss on a rotting log or tree base. Species-level ID would require chemical spot tests and a close look at whether the cup surface is granular-soredate or corticate-squamulose, so I have kept it at genus.

Forest floor leaf litter (oak and maple leaves) with a dark, blackened, decaying mushroom cap and a small tan button-shaped fungus to its left. Neither shows gills, pores, stipe, or spore print, so no identification beyond 'a decayed agaric-type fungus' is possible from this angle.

Backlit canopy/habitat shot looking up through a mixed deciduous crown; some leaves appear palmately lobed (maple-like, possibly Acer rubrum or A. pensylvanicum) but every leaf is silhouetted against sky with no bark, twig, or fruit detail. Not identifiable beyond 'broadleaf forest canopy' — a photo of a low branch showing leaf arrangement (opposite vs alternate) and lobe shape would settle it.

Habitat shot of an eroded trail with exposed tree roots, compacted soil, scattered grass tufts and a mat of green pleurocarpous moss over the roots. No flowering structures, leaves or sporophytes are resolvable, so nothing can be named below the level of 'moss' — a close-up of leaf shape and capsules would be needed for genus. [Catalogue entry "Trailside Moss (unidentified)" removed: 'Bryophyta sp.' is a rank above genus, not an organism. This photo remains unidentified.]

Bark-only photo of a mature trunk (~40+ cm diameter) with long, narrow vertical plates that curl loose at the edges, giving a shaggy look; no leaves, twigs, buds, or fruit are visible on the subject tree, so this cannot be taken past 'unidentified hardwood.' The shagginess fits an old red maple (Acer rubrum) or a large aspen/poplar, and superficially resembles shagbark hickory (Carya ovata); a look up at the canopy leaves or a fallen leaf at the base would settle it. [Catalogue entry "Unidentified mature hardwood (bark only)" removed: "unidentified" in the name — a description of the photo, not a taxon. This photo remains unidentified.]

Mixed-forest interior shot taken from below: a young conifer with self-pruned, persistent dead lower branches occupies the foreground, with maple-leaved hardwoods and gray-barked trunks behind. No close view of needles, cones, buds or bark texture, so the conifer can only be called a spruce/fir/hemlock-type evergreen — a branchlet showing needle cross-section (four-sided and sharp = spruce, flat and blunt with white bands = fir or hemlock) would settle it. Nothing here suggests a regulated invasive.

Extreme close-up of a young, warty, downy follicle (seed pod) with a curved beak on a stout hairy stalk, backed by a large entire leaf with a pale midrib — consistent with Common Milkweed in mid-August. No flowers, full leaf arrangement, or sap visible, so species is inferred from pod texture and habit.

Two flat-topped white compound umbels with finely divided ferny foliage at the grassy edge of a goldenrod stand — classic wild carrot. Umbels are still flat/open rather than curled into a bird's nest; no purple central floret visible at this resolution.

This is a habitat/landscape shot of a second-growth mixed hardwood understory along an old dry-laid stone wall and rubble pile. The central tree has smooth-to-shallowly ridged gray bark with epicormic sprouts bearing ovate, pinnately veined, serrate leaves, and the shoot near the trunk looks possibly pinnately compound (ash-like), but no bud, twig, fruit, or clear leaf-arrangement detail is visible, so I cannot key it past 'unidentified hardwood'. Nothing here clearly reads as a watchlist invasive, though the leafy shrub at right could be a bush honeysuckle or glossy buckthorn — check for opposite leaves and hollow pith (honeysuckle) versus alternate leaves with 8+ parallel vein pairs and thornless twigs (buckthorn) to settle it.

This is a wide habitat shot of a disturbed, eroded gully with an exposed pipe or culvert at the woodland edge, not a photo of a single specimen. Several plants are present — narrow-leaved herbs at left that could be goldenrod (Solidago), a leafy rosette-like stem in the center foreground, brambles and young hardwood saplings — but none is shown close enough (no flowers, no leaf detail, no stem view) to key reliably. Worth a return visit: disturbed soil around culverts is exactly where Japanese knotweed, bush honeysuckle, and glossy buckthorn establish, and the coarse-leaved shrubby growth mid-frame cannot be ruled out from this distance; a close photo of leaf arrangement (alternate vs. opposite) and stem (hollow and jointed vs. solid) would settle it.

Photo appears inverted/rotated: leaf litter and stipe bases occupy the upper frame with a colony of lacy, finely divided fern fronds below. Only distant, out-of-focus blades are shown — no pinnule detail, rachis grooving, or sori are visible, so this cannot be taken past 'fern'. The overall lacy, twice-to-thrice-cut look and dense colonial habit is consistent with hay-scented fern (Dennstaedtia punctilobula) or lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), but the photo does not settle it. [Catalogue entry "Fern (unidentified colony)" removed: 'Polypodiopsida sp.' is a rank above genus, not an organism. This photo remains unidentified.]

Habitat shot of a cobble/sand beach with a single isolated clump of coarse grass at the tide line; too distant to see ligules, spikelets or rhizomes. Salt-tolerant shoreline grass, most likely a cordgrass (Spartina/Sporobolus), but a photo of the inflorescence and leaf base is needed to confirm even the genus.

Single erect unbranched flowering spike with dense terminal raceme and thick, pale, felted leaves clasping/decurrent down the stem, growing on an open cobble/gravel shoreline — consistent with common mullein (Verbascum thapsus). Photo is distant, so the woolly hairs and yellow corollas can't be resolved; check for dense star-shaped hairs on the leaf surface to confirm. Goldenrod in flower at right edge.

Single tall unbranched flowering stalk with dense club-like terminal spike, thick woolly grey-green leaves clasping and running down the stem in the basal rosette — classic Common Mullein on a rip-rap shoreline. Spike is past peak bloom (mostly seed capsules) in mid-August.

Stand of stout unbranched stems with opposite, broadly oblong leaves showing thick pink-red midribs and pale undersides, at a gravel roadside edge — classic Asclepias syriaca. No flowers or pods visible, but leaf shape, venation and growth habit are diagnostic.

Upright square-ish stems carrying interrupted whorls of small pale-pink flowers in the leaf axils, with narrow toothed, somewhat hairy leaves — this reads as a mint (Mentha sp.), most likely wild mint (M. canadensis) or an escaped M. arvensis/spicata. Species cannot be settled from this photo; crushing a leaf for the characteristic mint scent and checking for a square stem and axillary (not terminal) flower whorls would confirm the genus. Not purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria, regulated): that has dense showy magenta terminal spikes, not small axillary whorls — worth a second look on site given the damp open habitat. Common milkweed leaves and reddish stems fill the upper left.

Slender reddish-purple stems 1-1.5 m tall carrying small pale-pink flowers in long interrupted leafy spikes, with narrow lanceolate sessile leaves — consistent with a thin, open-grown Purple Loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria), a Maine-regulated invasive, so flagging it despite low confidence. What would settle it: check stem cross-section (Lythrum is squarish/4-6 angled and downy), leaves opposite or whorled and clasping with rounded bases, and flowers with 5-6 crinkled magenta petals; if instead the flowers have 4 notched petals over a long slender seed capsule the plant is a Willowherb (Epilobium), which is what the sparse bloom could also indicate. Broad oval leaves on a red stem at upper left are Common Milkweed.

Arching rose canes in coastal grassland with immature green-to-orange hips, persistent long-tipped sepals, and shiny serrate pinnate leaves (5-7 leaflets) — consistent with the existing Wild Rose (Rosa sp.) entry, likely Rosa virginiana. Hips are smooth and globose rather than the large fat wrinkled-leaf hips of invasive Rosa rugosa; leaflet gloss and stipule shape would settle species.

This is a habitat shot of a dense low tangle of mixed broadleaf seedlings, herbs and grass beneath a large rough-barked tree (possibly an old apple, given the fallen fruit-like object at lower centre). No flowers, fruit or clear single subject are resolvable, and several species are intergrown, so no genus can be assigned. A single orange pendant flower at mid-left appears to be jewelweed. To make this identifiable, photograph one plant at a time: a close view of a leaf showing margin and arrangement, plus stem and any flower or fruit.

Small madder-family herb growing in gravel at a building edge: leaves in whorls of 4-6, narrow and bristle-tipped, with tiny 4-lobed pale pink/white flowers sitting in leafy clusters at the shoot tips — the pattern of Sherardia arvensis (field madder). Species is not certain from this angle; a close look at whether the flowers sit inside a ring of involucral leaves (Sherardia) versus in open branched sprays (Galium) would settle it. Palmately lobed leaves upper left (a Geranium or buttercup) were too indistinct to name.

Erect gravel-edge weed with opposite lance-shaped leaves, tiny notched pinkish-white flowers, and the diagnostic long slender inferior ovaries (young seed pods) below each flower — Epilobium, matching the existing willowherb entry. Broadleaf plantain rosettes and a Rubus cane are in the foreground.

The tall central plant has opposite, sessile, lance-shaped leaves on a reddish erect stem with small pale pink four-petaled flowers and slender developing capsules in the upper axils — consistent with Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum) already in the guide. Broadleaf plantain rosettes and a toothed dandelion-type rosette carpet the gravel around it.

Erect stem against the plywood with opposite-to-alternate narrow lance-shaped leaves, small four-petaled pinkish flowers and long slender ascending seed capsules — consistent with Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum) already in the guide. Broad-leaved plantain rosettes and dandelion foliage fill the gravel edge around it.

Erect stem against building foundation with opposite, sessile lance-shaped leaves and small pale pink four-petaled flowers on slender ovaries — consistent with Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum). Surrounding gravel is carpeted with broadleaf plantain rosettes, a dandelion-type toothed leaf, and a young Rubus cane at right.

Slender erect stem with narrow lanceolate opposite-to-alternate leaves, tiny pale pink 4-petalled notched flowers and long thin ascending seed capsules — classic Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum) growing in gravel at a building edge. Species-level ID would need a look at stigma shape and stem hairs.

Erect herb with opposite lance-shaped leaves, small four-petalled pale pink flowers, and long slender linear ovaries/capsules below each flower — the classic Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum) growing in gravel at a building edge. Broadleaf plantain rosettes with flower spikes, a dandelion rosette, and a Rubus cane are in the surrounding disturbed ground.

Slender erect plant with mostly opposite, sessile, toothed lanceolate leaves and tiny 4-petaled notched pink flowers borne on top of very long thin inferior ovaries (the 'stalks' below each flower) — classic Epilobium, likely E. ciliatum. Broadleaf plantain rosette in the foreground and a Rubus cane leaf at right.

Sprawling roadside stems with reddish, purple-tinged stalks, alternate narrow lance-shaped leaves, and terminal racemes of long slender red seed capsules — consistent with fireweed past flowering. Flowers are gone, so species is inferred from the capsule spikes and leaf shape rather than petals; a lingering pink 4-petalled flower would confirm.

Sprawling herb with opposite sessile leaves, five-petaled yellow flowers and abundant reddening three-parted seed capsules on branched cymes — consistent with common St. John's Wort in mid-August seed set. Orange spurred flowers of jewelweed and whorled bedstraw foliage are mixed into the same patch.

Low, spreading shrub with simple, entire, elliptic-ovate leaves in opposite pairs crowded at the twig tips, pale grey-green and softly hairy-looking, growing in a shaded woodland edge with grass and leaf litter — consistent with invasive bush honeysuckle (Lonicera morrowii/tatarica). No flowers or fruit are present, so this is a tentative call; snap a twig to check for the hollow brown pith (honeysuckle) versus solid white pith, and look for silky white 'threads' when a leaf is torn slowly, which would instead indicate Cornus (dogwood). Because this is a Maine Do Not Sell species, it is flagged for a follow-up visit when berries are on.

Lacy, yellow-green, broadly triangular twice-cut fronds held nearly horizontally in a loose colony on dry hardwood-forest floor litter — consistent with hay-scented fern. Rachis/scale detail and crushed-frond scent are not verifiable from the photo, so New York fern (fronds tapering to tiny pinnae at the base) should be ruled out on the ground.

A single lacy, finely divided fern crown in oak/beech leaf litter, photographed from above. The frond outline reads roughly triangular and twice-to-thrice cut, which is consistent with either Dennstaedtia punctilobula (hay-scented fern) or a young Dryopteris (intermedia/carthusiana), but the underside sori, the scales and colour of the stipe base, and whether the plant is clump-forming or spreading from a creeping rhizome are all not visible, and a crush-and-smell test (hay-scented fern's sweet cut-hay odour) was not recorded. Nothing here suggests a watchlist invasive.

Slender erect herb with broad ovate leaves and a terminal spike-like raceme bearing one small pale blue-violet flower, growing in a grassy, leaf-littered woodland edge. The image is out of focus at the flower, so corolla shape, leaf arrangement (opposite vs. alternate) and calyx details cannot be resolved; candidates include Lobelia, Scutellaria and Physostegia, and a sharp close-up of a single flower and of the stem node would settle it. Nothing here suggests a regulated invasive.

Central plant shows an erect square stem with widely spaced opposite lance-shaped leaves and a dense terminal bracted spike bearing a pale violet two-lipped flower — consistent with Prunella vulgaris in a shaded forest-edge opening.
Low-growing plant with opposite lance-shaped leaves and a dense terminal spike of two-lipped violet flowers with a hooded upper lip — Prunella vulgaris, already in the guide.

Severely motion-blurred shot of a wooded slope with fallen branches and mixed green understory; no leaf shape, flower, or bark detail is resolvable, so no taxon can be named. A re-shoot with the camera steady and a single plant filling the frame would be needed.

Screened out: The subject of the photograph is an animal (a small mammal, apparently a squirrel or similar, perched on a log) rather than plants, fungi, or vegetation; surrounding foliage is blurred background only.

Cluster of heart- to kidney-shaped, crenate-margined leaves on long petioles arising from a basal cluster on the forest floor — consistent with a violet (Viola sp.). No flowers or capsules are visible, so species cannot be determined; a bloom (color, spurred lower petal) or the presence of a leafy aerial stem vs. purely basal leaves would settle it.

Blurry close-up of alternate, ovate, coarsely and bluntly toothed pale-green leaves on a translucent succulent stem with a swollen node, plus a rounded green structure at lower left consistent with a jewelweed flower bud or immature seed capsule. No open flower is visible, so the ID rests on leaf shape, tooth pattern and stem texture; a spurred orange flower or an exploding capsule would confirm it.

Severely out-of-focus view of a mossy forest floor with leaf litter between two tree trunks. No leaf, stem, or reproductive detail is resolvable, and the green mat could be moss, algae, or low herbaceous growth — nothing supports even a genus.

Clusters of thin, concentrically zoned, wavy-margined bracket fungi fruiting on a fallen white birch log, with green algal film on older caps — consistent with the weathered Trametes/Trichaptum brackets already catalogued. Pore surface is not visible in this photo, so species (e.g. true Trametes versicolor) cannot be confirmed.

A single young bracket emerging from a fallen white birch log — smooth, pale tan, kidney-shaped cap with a lumpy surface and amber guttation droplets at the margin, all consistent with young Fomitopsis (Piptoporus) betulina. Pore surface is not visible in this photo, so the ID rests on host and cap appearance.

A single small, smooth, tan-brown knob-like bracket emerging from a fallen white birch log lying in leaf litter; the birch substrate plus the smooth kidney-shaped young cap fits birch polypore. Underside and pore surface are not visible, which is what would confirm it.

A single fallen acorn (scaly cap uppermost, smooth green nut below) resting on a mossy stone; blurred and with no leaves or twig in frame, so only the genus is supportable and even that rests on the cap texture. If it is instead a small orange-capped mushroom the ID would change entirely — check for gills/pores underneath and whether the 'cap' is a woody cupule of overlapping scales.

Image is entirely out of focus — only pale tan and cream blurs over what may be leaf litter or dry ground. No leaf shape, margin, venation, flower or fruit is resolvable, so no genus can be assigned. A re-shoot with the camera focused on a single structure is needed.

Small yellow five-petaled flower above trifoliate, heart-shaped (obcordate) leaflets on a tiny plant in leaf litter — classic yellow wood sorrel (Oxalis). Species-level ID (O. stricta vs O. dillenii) would need a look at seed capsule pubescence and stipules; acorns and grass blades also in frame.

Small five-petaled yellow flower above clover-like leaves of three heart-shaped (notched) leaflets on a slender reddish stem, growing through leaf litter — Oxalis stricta. An oak acorn cap lies beside it; no oak foliage visible to key the oak.

Fallen acorns on a bare trail surface — nuts with shallow, tightly scaled cups identify them as Quercus, but no leaves or bark are in frame so the species cannot be pinned down (small size and shallow cup suggest red oak group). Fine grass blades at top right are unrelated.

Small conifer sapling with whorled branches and flat, two-ranked sprays of blunt needles on a stout upright leader — consistent with a young balsam fir; image is blurred so needle undersides (two white stomatal bands, resinous fragrance) could not be checked to rule out eastern hemlock, which has finer, shorter needles with tiny stalks and a nodding leader.

Forest-floor litter of fallen oak leaves with two shed acorns (nut plus shallow scaly cup) directly below; the leaves are deeply lobed with rounded, bristle-less tips suggesting the white oak group, but the leaves are bleached and skeletonized so I am keeping this at genus. A hairy caterpillar (a tussock-type larva, possibly browntail moth, whose hairs cause a rash in coastal Maine) is crawling on a twig in the frame — do not handle.

Heavily out-of-focus forest floor: leaf litter, dead twigs, a fallen log, a small unidentified broadleaf sapling shoot at top and a yellow-orange fungal patch at bottom edge. Nothing is sharp enough to key — no clear leaf shape, margin, venation, or fungal cap/pore detail. A focused close-up of the sapling leaves (arrangement and margin) or of the yellow fungus (underside) would be needed.

Basal rosettes of long-petioled, heart-shaped to ovate leaves with shallowly crenate margins on the forest floor — consistent with a stemless violet (Viola sp.). No flowers or fruit present, so species cannot be determined; flower colour and whether leaves are hairy would settle it.

A dense basal cluster of long-petioled, heart-shaped (cordate) leaves with crenate margins rising from a single crown on shaded forest floor — consistent with a violet (Viola sp.). No flowers or capsules are present, so species cannot be settled; leaf shape/pubescence and flower colour in spring would separate V. sororia from V. labradorica/V. cucullata.

A single firm, rootless, unstalked ball-shaped fungus with a tan-ochre rind broken into small dark warts/areolae, sitting on soil at the base of a mossy granite boulder. Warted rind and lack of any stalk or apical pore point to Scleroderma (earthball); slicing it to reveal a solid purple-black interior would confirm it and rule out a true edible puffball.
Basal rosette of broad, oval, strongly parallel-veined leaves with long petioles and a tall dense cylindrical flower spike on a leafless scape — classic Plantago major on a compacted trail edge.

Close view of a finely twice-cut fern frond with a pale yellowish-green, minutely hairy rachis and pinnules whose lobes are cut nearly to the midvein — consistent with hay-scented fern, the best match among existing entries. Full frond outline, the base/stipe scales, and the underside sori are not visible, so lady fern (Athyrium, grooved glabrous rachis with scaly base) and New York fern (pinnae tapering to nothing at the base) cannot be fully ruled out; crushing a pinna for the hay-like scent would settle it. Nothing on the invasive watchlist here.

A single pinnate-pinnatifid frond with light yellow-green, once-lobed pinnae bearing blunt, entire rounded lobes and a pale straw-colored rachis — consistent with the marsh/New York fern group (Thelypteris s.l. / Parathelypteris). Species cannot be settled without seeing whether the lower pinnae taper to tiny nubs (New York fern) and whether the frond base and sori are visible, so genus only.

Dense colony of lacy, yellow-green, twice-cut fronds with slender straw-colored stipes and finely dissected pinnules, matching hay-scented fern; a crushed-frond sniff (sweet hay smell) and hairy rachis would confirm, and rule out New York fern, whose pinnae taper toward the frond base and which is only once-pinnate-pinnatifid.

Only the mid-portion of a single finely-divided (2-pinnate to pinnate-pinnatifid) fern blade is in focus, with a pale yellowish-green rachis; no frond outline, stipe base, scales, or sori/indusia are visible, and the underside was not photographed. Habit is consistent with either hay-scented fern (Dennstaedtia) or lady fern (Athyrium), but the features that separate them — glandular hairiness and crushed-hay smell versus grooved green/straw stipe with dark scales and hooked sori — cannot be checked from this image. Nothing here suggests a watchlist invasive.

A single firm, unstalked yellowish-tan ball sitting on leaf litter, its surface broken into small warty/areolate scales — characteristic of a Scleroderma earthball rather than a true puffball. Interior was not cut, which is the check that would settle it (earthballs have a solid black-purple gleba even when young).

Several small white, smooth, kidney-shaped fungal caps emerging along the side of a decaying log, seen only from above and slightly out of focus. Without a view of the underside (gills vs. pores), stipe attachment, flesh texture, or spore print, this cannot be placed even to genus — candidates range from young Pleurotus/Crepidotus-type shelf fungi to a white Tyromyces-like polypore. Re-photograph the fertile surface from below.

Young erect stem bearing two whorls of three leaflets; leaflets glossy, irregularly few-toothed/lobed with the terminal leaflet on a noticeably longer stalk and lateral leaflets nearly sessile — classic Toxicodendron radicans. Absence of thorns and of a shrubby many-leafleted rachis rules out young Rubus or ash.

Upward canopy shot of a large multi-stemmed hardwood with furrowed gray bark; the foliage is backlit and out of focus, and no leaf, twig, bud, or fruit detail is resolvable. Some crown leaves suggest a maple, but nothing in the frame confirms genus, so no name is entered. A close photo of a leaf (arrangement, lobing, margin) and of the trunk bark at eye level would settle it.

Broad oval leaves with strong parallel arcuate veins in a basal rosette, plus slender dense flower/seed spikes on leafless stalks — Plantago major. A yellow tussock-type caterpillar is resting on one leaf; ferns fill the background.

Screened out: The photo shows a close-up of a laminated interpretive sign/placard with printed graphics and text; vegetation appears only as blurred background, so there is no identifiable plant subject.

Several waxy, pure-white, leafless stems with single nodding bell-shaped flowers pushing up through hardwood leaf litter — classic Monotropa uniflora. The broad parallel-veined green leaves around it are Canada mayflower (Maianthemum canadense), not part of this plant.

Photo shows a dark, crumbly, blackish-brown swelling on the trunk of a smooth-barked sapling in mixed conifer/hardwood woods. It could be a sterile conk (e.g. chaga, Inonotus obliquus, typical on birch) or simply a burl/canker; the image is too soft to read the host bark (birch vs. other hardwood), there is no visible pore surface or interior color, and no leaves attached to this stem, so neither the tree nor the growth can be named. A close shot of the host bark and leaves plus the cut/broken interior of the mass (orange-brown corky flesh would indicate chaga) would settle it.
Screened out: Photograph of an interpretive sign panel showing artwork of birds (ducks/seabirds) mounted on a wooden frame; no plants, fungi, or vegetation are the subject.

A small bright orange-red fungus is partly visible among grass and moss, but the photo is out of focus and the cap surface, gill attachment, stem and spore-bearing surface cannot be seen. It could be a waxcap (Hygrocybe), a Cordyceps-type club, or an orange Cladonia-associated fruiting body — no genus can be supported. A sharp shot from the side plus a view of the underside would settle it.

A bright orange, lobed/wavy-capped fungus fruiting in haircap moss (Polytrichum) and reindeer-type Cladonia among hardwood leaf litter. Only the upper surface is visible — the hymenium (gills, false gills, pores, or a gelatinous jelly texture) is not shown, and there is no view of the stipe, base, or flesh, so it cannot be placed even to genus. Candidates spanning very different groups (Cantharellus, Hygrophoropsis, Dacrymyces/Tremella, an orange Hygrocybe) cannot be separated from this angle; a photo of the underside and a cut section would settle it.

A single small orange-capped mushroom on a mossy, rocky slope, but the image is out of focus at the cap and the stem base, gills/pores, and any veil or volva are hidden — not enough to place it even in a genus (orange-capped Russula, Amanita, Hygrocybe and Lactarius all remain possible). A photo showing the underside, a full longitudinal section, and the base in the substrate would settle it. Moss and a small unidentified compound leaf are also present but likewise not identifiable here.

Small white coral fungi erupting from a moss-covered rotting log; the branch tips end in tiny crown-like rings of points, which is the key mark for Artomyces pyxidatus. Tips are slightly blurred, so Clavulina/Ramaria cannot be ruled out with certainty — a close look at whether each tip is a flat crown of 3-6 prongs would settle it.

Two small bright orange-capped mushrooms in hardwood leaf litter, but the photo is blurred, shot from above, and no gills, stem base, or flesh are visible. Orange caps of this size could be Hygrocybe/Hygrophorus (waxcap), Amanita muscaria var. guessowii button, Leccinum, or a Marasmius relative — a side view showing gill attachment, stem surface, and any ring or volva would settle it.

Badly blurred close-up of a decaying tree trunk with rot-stained bark and what may be weathered bracket fungi at lower left; no cap surface, pore layer, or bark/leaf detail is resolvable, and the tree cannot be named from this image. A sharper photo of the bracket's underside and of the tree's leaves would settle both.

A pale grey-white, densely branched cushion about 5 cm across sitting on oak leaf litter. The chalky, non-fleshy look and the hollow, perforated, dichotomously branching axils point to a Cladonia (reindeer/cup lichen group) rather than a plant; I could not get species from this angle, and a grey coral fungus (Clavulina cinerea) cannot be fully ruled out without seeing whether the branches are brittle and hollow (lichen) or soft and solid (fungus). It is not the cup-bearing pixie cup already catalogued, so it is entered separately.
Screened out: Image shows bare gravelly ground with twigs and rock fragments at night; no plant or fungus is the subject and no vegetation is identifiable.

Weathered, dark grey-brown shelving bracket fungi at the base of a hardwood trunk; caps are dust-covered and the pore surface is not visible, so no genus can be confirmed. Matches the existing 'small bracket fungi (weathered)' catalogue entry rather than supporting a new name — a look at the underside (pore size, gill-like teeth vs round pores) and a fresh margin would be needed.

A small woody seedling on the forest floor among oak leaf litter and acorn caps; the ovate, long-petioled, crenate-toothed leaves with a slightly flattened petiole read as a young aspen (Populus) sprout, so I have matched the existing aspen entry rather than create a duplicate. Confidence is low because juvenile Populus, Tilia americana and young Betula seedlings overlap in leaf shape — bark, catkins, or a mature crown would settle it; no invasive-watchlist candidate is suggested here.

A single waxy, leafless white stem with a nodding terminal flower rising from acorn-littered hardwood duff — classic Monotropa uniflora (ghost pipe). A fern frond (unidentified from this angle) and acorns/oak leaves share the frame.

A ground-level colony of large heart-shaped (cordate), shallowly toothed long-petioled leaves spreading over disturbed gravelly ground with oak leaf litter — consistent with a coltsfoot (Tussilago farfara) patch in late-summer leaf-only stage. No flowers or leaf undersides are shown; turning a leaf to check for dense white felt beneath (and the reddish-scaled petiole) would confirm it against a violet (Viola sp.) rosette, whose leaves are smaller, glabrous and green beneath.

Shade-forest herb on leaf litter with a single erect stem, paired broadly ovate, shallowly toothed leaves on short petioles, and a tight terminal cluster of tiny green unopened flower buds — consistent with Circaea (enchanter's nightshade). Open flowers or the hooked-bristly fruits would confirm the genus and separate C. canadensis from C. alpina; without them this stays tentative.

Blurry but shows opposite, coarsely toothed ovate leaves with small pale pink/purple two-lipped flowers in axillary whorls, matching hemp-nettle (Galeopsis tetrahit) already in the guide; stem bristles/swollen nodes not resolvable at this focus.

Vegetative shoot with a single unbranched stem and alternate, sessile, narrowly lance-shaped entire leaves with a strong midrib and faint lateral veins — consistent with a goldenrod (Solidago) rosette-stage stem in mid-August before budding. No inflorescence, so an aster (Symphyotrichum) or flat-topped goldenrod (Euthamia, which would have resin dots and 1–3 parallel veins) cannot be excluded; a return visit at flowering, or checking for three prominent parallel veins and rough leaf margins, would settle it.

Yellow dandelion-like composite heads (all ray florets, notched ray tips) on a slender leafy stem with alternate, sessile, coarsely and irregularly toothed lance-shaped leaves on forest-edge leaf litter — consistent with a hawkweed (Hieracium, in the H. umbellatum/kalmii group). Species is not settlable from this blurry image; involucre hairs, leaf pubescence and whether basal leaves persist would be needed, so left at genus.

A single brown-capped mushroom seen only from above, growing in packed gravel/soil among grass. No view of the underside (gills vs. pores), stem, base, or spore-print, so even the genus cannot be supported — it could be a bolete, a Cortinarius, a Lactarius, or a tricholomatoid species. Someone should return and photograph the underside and the stem base.
Screened out: The image is dominated by an interpretive display board/signage rather than vegetation; the surrounding plants are incidental and too partial to serve as a survey record.
Opposite, thick oval leaves with pale midrib on a stout unbranched stem, bearing a single young warty follicle (pod) — Common Milkweed in fruit.

Dense stand of goldenrod in early bloom: lance-shaped, sharply toothed, three-nerved leaves on unbranched stems with one-sided plume-like flower clusters just opening — consistent with the Solidago canadensis complex already catalogued.

Flat-topped (corymbiform) clusters of white ray flowers with yellow discs on reddish-purple stems, with entire, lance-shaped leaves tapering at both ends — consistent with Doellingeria umbellata. A small bee is on one head; unopened buds fill much of the cluster. Background yellow-budded plumes appear to be goldenrod.
Five-petaled yellow flowers with a bushy tuft of many stamens, opposite small oblong leaves, and reddish-brown seed capsules on branching cymes — matches the existing St. John's Wort entry.

Sprawling vine with many-paired pinnate leaflets ending in branched tendrils, climbing over surrounding vegetation, with a small violet-blue pea flower cluster at right — Vicia sp. (cow/hairy vetch group). Bramble (Rubus) leaves and fern fronds fill the background.

Palmately compound leaves in threes and fives with toothed, wrinkled leaflets, whitish undersides and reddish canes — a Rubus cane (raspberry/blackberry group); no fruit or prickle detail to fix species.

Erect shrub with a narrow pyramidal panicle of small white-to-pink-tinged 5-petaled flowers and sharply toothed, short-stalked alternate leaves — Spiraea, almost certainly the native meadowsweet (S. alba var. latifolia). Species-level confirmation would need a clear look at whether the young stems are angled/reddish and hairless (latifolia) versus round and downy (S. alba s.s.); the surrounding goldenrod is in bud/early bloom.

A single leafy shoot with a reddish, apparently jointed stem and large alternate ovate-acuminate leaves with strong pinnate venation, growing in a grassy roadside/field edge; no flowers or fruit are visible, so this is only a tentative genus call. It resembles a young Japanese/Bohemian knotweed shoot (a regulated invasive) — the settling features are a hollow stem, a swollen node with a thin papery sheath (ocrea) at each leaf base, and a flat or squared-off leaf base. Please recheck this stem for those; if leaf bases taper and there is no ocrea, it is not knotweed.

Tall field grass photographed from below at seed stage: stout culms with broad, flat, blue-green leaves and narrow, contracted straw-coloured panicles held above the sward — consistent with reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea), which forms exactly this kind of dense monoculture in damp open field edges. Calamagrostis canadensis (bluejoint) is the main alternative and would have finer, more open, purplish-tinged panicles and softer, narrower leaves; a close look at the ligule (long, membranous and blunt in Phalaris, shorter in Calamagrostis) and at whether the panicle branches spread at flowering would settle it. Flagging because aggressive Eurasian genotypes of reed canary grass are a wetland-invasion concern in Maine.

Tall shrub with alternate, entire, glossy obovate leaves showing 7-9 pairs of strongly parallel, upcurved lateral veins, and small berries in axillary clusters ripening red then black — this keys to glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus), a Maine Do-Not-Sell invasive. Worth confirming on the ground: leaf margin must be untoothed, twigs thornless with naked (scaleless) buds, and inner bark yellow-orange when scratched. If leaves prove finely toothed and berries hang in an elongated raceme, it is chokecherry (Prunus virginiana) instead.

Shrubby dogwood in fruit: opposite-to-crowded ovate leaves with strongly arcuate veins, bright red fruit stalks (pedicels) and dark blue-purple drupes — consistent with Cornus amomum/alternifolia group; species not separable here without a clear view of leaf arrangement along the stem and twig pith colour. Matches the existing Cornus sp. entry.
